title: As a Kenyan who’s been shaped by both my Indian heritage and global influences, I used to lean heavily toward the Democrats, supporting their focus on social justice and equality. When Trump won the presidency, I was genuinely surprised. Like many others at the time, I couldn’t understand why Americans had chosen someone who seemed to represent such divisive ideas. I was strongly opposed to his rhetoric and saw his victory as a backward step. But over the years, my perspective has shifted, and it wasn't due to Trump himself but rather due to the far-left movement. A significant factor in my change of heart was the way the far left has handled issues around gender. While I still support equality, their rhetoric on gender began to feel excessive. I started to feel like the far left was pushing an agenda that wasn’t based in reality, particularly when it came to discussions about gender identity. The argument that gender is entirely a social construct, separate from biological sex, felt too extreme to me. While I acknowledge that gender identity can be a complex issue, some of the ideas the far left promotes didn’t align with my understanding of basic biology. The far left also seemed to push this narrative in a way that left little room for debate. It became a question of accepting these ideas without question, and if you didn’t, you were labeled intolerant or bigoted. This approach felt dogmatic, as though they were demanding total agreement, which made me uncomfortable. I believe in equality, but I also believe in the importance of open discussion, where different viewpoints can be heard and respected. This rigidity made me question whether the far left was more focused on pushing an ideological agenda than on fostering meaningful change. At the same time, I began to reconsider some of the ideas coming from the right. I don’t agree with everything Trump represents, and many of his policies wouldn’t directly affect me here in Kenya. But what I did start to appreciate was his challenge to some of the more extreme ideas coming from the left. Trump’s policies, particularly his nationalist approach, started to make more sense to me in contrast to the far left’s cultural push. While I don’t support all his actions or ideas, I found that he offered a perspective that seemed more grounded in reality, at least compared to the far-left extremes. For example, while Trump’s policies on immigration or the economy might not directly impact me, I did appreciate his rejection of political correctness and his defense of traditional values. His approach felt more practical, especially when compared to the far-left's push to reshape society according to ideas I couldn’t agree with. This doesn’t mean I fully support everything Trump stands for, but his stance on certain cultural issues resonated with me in a way the far-left’s positions no longer did. What ultimately pushed me away from the far left was their growing insistence on pushing a single narrative on gender issues and the refusal to engage in open debate. It wasn’t that I suddenly became a conservative, but I found myself rejecting the extremes of the left, which felt out of touch with reality. I believe in fairness, equality, and social progress, but I also believe in having discussions where differing viewpoints can be explored, not silenced. Over time, I’ve shifted toward the political center and now lean moderately right. It’s not because I’ve adopted conservative views on everything, but because I’ve grown tired of the far left’s extreme positions, particularly on cultural issues like gender. In a world where political discussions are often polarized, I’ve come to appreciate a more balanced approach, where ideas are debated openly, and not every disagreement leads to labels or judgment. My move away from the far left wasn’t about any particular policy that impacted me directly. It was more about rejecting the cultural direction they’ve taken, particularly on gender issues. The rhetoric they push just doesn’t seem true to me, and I feel more comfortable aligning with a more moderate position that allows for diverse opinions without imposing a single narrative.

So, the bottom line is not cleared from salary and compensation related expenses of the laid off employees even in this quarter (but maybe in China).
